content.label: Rollout stages and the canary gate
content.takeaway: Internal → canary → general availability; a flag leaves canary only through the gate.

nodes.title: Three stages: internal, canary, general availability

content.markdown:
- **Internal:** staff accounts only, so colleagues hit problems before customers (usually one working day; no minimum).
- **Canary:** a small share of real traffic.
- **General availability:** everyone, in steps of 25%, 50% and 100%.

Every move is recorded in the rollout tool.

nodes.title: Canary: 5% of requests for at least 30 minutes

content.markdown: Requests are picked at random per request, not per user. The window covers a full traffic cycle of the slowest endpoint, and a manual change to the percentage restarts it. Short canaries are the most common way a bad flag reaches general availability.

nodes.title: A flag leaves canary only when the metrics check passes

content.markdown: The rollout tool runs the check at the end of the canary window: error rate and p95 latency of flagged requests against the same requests over the previous 7 days. If it fails, the flag stays in canary and the owner investigates before trying again.

content.label: Safety nets: kill switch and monitoring
content.takeaway: Turning a flag off is always safe; watch the dashboard while it ramps up.

nodes.title: Every flag needs a kill switch that turns it off within 1 minute

content.markdown: Tested in staging before canary and recorded in the rollout tool: a flag without a tested kill switch cannot enter canary. Anyone on the owning team may use it without approval. Turning the flag back on restarts the rollout from the internal stage.

nodes.title: During the ramp-up, watch the error dashboard

content.markdown: Page the on-call engineer if errors rise. Flagged and unflagged requests sit side by side, so a gap points at the flag, not the platform. Keep watching until the flag has been at 100% for one hour.

content.label: After rollout: flag cleanup
content.takeaway: Flags that are fully on don't stay in the code.

nodes.title: Remove a flag from the code 30 days after it is fully on

content.markdown: The owner opens a cleanup ticket at 100%, linked to the rollout record. Flags past the deadline appear in the weekly stale-flag report: old flags make the code harder to read and slow every later rollout.
